extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of literary criticism, philosophy, and biblical interpretation; literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for critics and readers on how to evaluate philosophical/scholarly works (especially on Spinoza and Biblical interpretation): what to look for in method, coherence, interpretive prudence, and the author's moral/edifying power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat each work as an independent whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The business of criticism is to deal with every independent work as an independent whole, rather than establishing relations between works which the author has not established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should not conflate separate works (e.g., the Tractatus Theologico-Politicus and the Ethics) or import axioms from one into the other; analyze the work on its own terms and locate any external supports in the author's other writings if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the author's spirit and tendencies rather than mere formulas
rubrics_metrics.description: A philosopher's real power over mankind resides not in his metaphysical formulas, but in the spirit and tendencies which have led him to adopt those formulas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating a thinker, bring to light the motivating spirit, aims, and tendencies that animate his formulas—these explain attraction and influence more than abstract propositions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seize the governing ideas that permeate an author's works
rubrics_metrics.description: Identify the 'important fact' or governing ideas that breathe through all the author's works and give them peculiar effect and power, even when not formally stated in a given work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look beyond isolated passages to the recurrent principles (e.g., denial of final causes, stoicism) that shape an author's outlook and explain recurring themes or emphases across different texts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish and make explicit methodological differences
rubrics_metrics.description: Note when an author deliberately uses different methods for different subjects (e.g., taking revelation 'as I found it' vs. arguing a priori about miracles).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should recognise and report methodological shifts (hypothesis-taking vs. a priori demonstration) and assess whether the author reconciles or justifies these differing approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demand coherence or account for apparent contradictions
rubrics_metrics.description: When an author makes assertions that appear contradictory (for example, presenting an event as miraculous in one place and asserting miracles are impossible in another), the critic should ask how these are reconciled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Either the author must reconcile them (e.g., treat certain recorded events as 'spurious additions') or criticism must expose the tension and trace its resolution (or lack thereof) in the author's thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discriminate among documentary sources; avoid treating disparate texts as equipollent
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not treat all parts of a corpus (e.g., the Bible) as of identical authority or character; distinguish documents of unequal value, applicability, and intent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-pattern of snatching an isolated text to support a thesis without checking context, the general drift of the scripture, or other passages of greater weight and authority; be wary of promoting conclusions drawn from chance expressions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Require that a work provide its own base/supports or seek them elsewhere
rubrics_metrics.description: If a work lacks the axioms, definitions, or supports needed for its speculative claims, critics should note that the base/supports are absent from the work itself and must be sought in the author's other writings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a speculative work appears 'in the air' or 'in want of a base,' criticism should either locate the missing foundations elsewhere in the author's corpus or mark the work as hypothethical and limited in scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate greatness by edifying power and moral influence, not mere novelty or following
rubrics_metrics.description: To be great, a philosopher must do more than circulate striking ideas; he must possess something that can influence character and is edifying — a noble, lofty 'grand style' that affects lives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the author's ideas inspire love, knowledge, or moral improvement in readers; note that fame can outlast schools of adherents if the work edifies and inspires powerful minds.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess moral systems for emotional efficacy for the masses
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral rules stated as ideas and followed rigorously are for the sage; the masses need a joyful, bounding emotion or inspiration (often provided by religion) to carry them along the narrow way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a moral or religious system, consider not only the intellectual rigour but also its capacity to generate the motivating emotions that enable ordinary people to practise virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid false identification or reductive labeling of an author
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not identify an author solely with a single doctrine or align him with extreme movements on the basis of a partial reading (e.g., denying final causes does not necessarily make one an atheist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place doctrines in context and resist simplistic parallels; recognise complexity (e.g., retaining the name of God while rejecting personified attributes) and avoid mischaracterisation by opponents or admirers.
